newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Siberians struggle to see comet during eclipse.
newsitem.headline: Siberians struggle to see comet during eclipse.

text.p: Scientists and local residents across Siberia and the Russian Far East watched a solar eclipse on Sunday that offered a rare opportunity to see a comet passing near the sun.
Scientists and tourists from across Russia as well as Japan, the United States and other nations travelled to the Siberian city of Chita and elsewhere to make observations.
"It was rather strange when it became dark," said Alexander Garetov, who saw the eclipse along with a group of tourists from Japan. "It was dark and it became colder."
He said the temperature was about -20 C before the eclipse and then fell by about five degrees.
Scientists said the eclipse offered only the third reported opportunity in the past 1,000 years to see a comet -- Comet Hale-Bopp -- with the naked eye during an eclipse.
But several people interviewed from the region said light cloud cover prevented an easy viewing of the comet.

"The sun started breaking out of the clouds just before the eclipse, so the comet was not visible with the naked eye," said Seiichiro Shibuya, a Japanese city government official making his ninth trip to see an eclipse.
"But in my group those with telescopes and binoculars could see the comet," he said.
Thousands of residents in Chita took to the streets to watch the two-minute, 18-second-long eclipse, during which the moon passed in front of the sun and brought darkness to the city.
The eclipse was seen in the Russian Far East and Siberia and small sections of northern China and Mongolia.
Several foreign tour companies brought tourists bearing special filters and cameras. Some school children from as far away as Moscow also made the long journey to the region to see the rare event.
John Frost, a Boston-area computer programmer who had previously seen five total eclipses, said he had planned a two-week holiday in Siberia with three other Americans.
Reached by telephone, he said the possibility of seeing the comet was an additional attraction. In the end he could not see it because of light cloud above a remote town near the Mongolian border.
Itar-Tass news agency said Russian military space officials were helping scientists study how the eclipse affected satellite navigation systems.
